{{Short description|Racial stereotype used in politics}}
{{pp-pc|small=yes}}
{{Redirect-distinguish-for|Angry white man|Angry young men|the 2013 book by sociologist Michael Kimmel|Angry White Men{{!}}''Angry White Men''|the 2016 book by Hsiao-Hung Pai|Angry White People{{!}}''Angry White People''}}
{{use mdy dates|date=September 2021}}
{{use American English|date=November 2018}}
"'''Angry white males'''" or "'''angry white men'''" is a term used in the [[English-speaking world]] to describe [[White people|white]] men who hold [[Right-wing politics|right-wing views]] and oppose [[Progressivism|progressive]] or [[Liberalism|liberal]] beliefs and policies. The term is most commonly used in [[Politics of the United States|American]] and [[Politics of Australia|Australian politics]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=Blake |first=John |date=2021-11-20 |title=There's nothing more frightening in America today than an angry White man |url=https://www.cnn.com/2021/11/20/us/angry-white-men-trials-blake-cec/index.html |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211120102712/https://www.cnn.com/2021/11/20/us/angry-white-men-trials-blake-cec/index.html |archive-date=November 20, 2021 |access-date=2022-08-08 |website=CNN |language=en}}</ref> In the United States, the term came into increasing use following white male backlash to the [[civil rights movement]] and [[second-wave feminism]] of the mid-20th century which gained more rights for white women and people of color in American society, in addition to [[immigration]], [[multiculturalism]] and [[LGBTQ rights by country or territory|LGBTQ rights]].<ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/news/made-by-history/wp/2017/08/29/why-are-so-many-white-men-so-angry/|title=Why are so many white men so angry? |date=2017-08-29 |author1=Steven M. Gillon |newspaper=[[The Washington Post]] |place=Washington, D.C. |issn=0190-8286 |oclc=1330888409}}</ref> Angry white men often blame their problems on non-whites, particularly non-white immigrants, [[Jews]], and [[African Americans]].<ref>{{cite web|url= https://books.google.com/books?id=CY8TAAAAQBAJ&pg=PT205|title= Angry White Men: American Masculinity at the End of an Era}}</ref>

== Theory ==
One of the major American political movements of 1992 was [[Feminism in the United States|women's rights]]. A reactionary backlash described by ''[[The Atlantic]]'' as the "Revolt of the Angry White Male" arose against the [[women's movement]].<ref name=atl>{{cite news |url=https://www.theatlantic.com/magazine/archive/1996/07/gap-politics/305579/ |title= Gap Politics |author= Steven Stark |date=July 1996 |work= The Atlantic }}</ref> The revolt of the angry white male quickly brought up questions and concerns that have long since haunted American politics.<ref name=atl/> Although, the primary concern regarding these questions has occurred since [[women's suffrage]], at least since the 1920s around women's rights to vote, they became prevalent again in the 1990s.<ref name=atl/> While the question was initially related to whether women would vote differently from men if given suffrage, otherwise known as the [[right to vote]], the [[gender pay gap]] gave new salience to women's rights issues.<ref name=atl/> While the issue of women's rights was a prevalent in the 1990s the movement of "Angry White Males" has grown substantially since.<ref name="auto"/>

More recently, Professor Bob Pease's view of the theory surrounding Angry White Male voters has stated that they see themselves as a [[voting bloc]] with their [[gender]] under attack which underscores why Angry White Male voters are more likely to feel politically disenfranchised and to therefore vote for [[Right-wing populism|right wing populist]] parties as a result.<ref name="auto">{{cite book |last= Noble|first= Carolyn |editor-first1= Carolyn |editor-first2= Goetz |editor-last1= Noble |editor-last2= Ottmann |date= 2020 |title=  The Challenge of Right-wing Nationalist Populism for Social Work |url= https://www.taylorfrancis.com/books/edit/10.4324/9780429056536/challenge-right-wing-nationalist-populism-social-work-carolyn-noble-goetz-ottmann?refId=ba183979-3c2c-4138-b3ba-f5647eeea075&context=ubx|location= London |publisher= Taylor & Francis|page= 55|doi= 10.4324/9780429056536 |isbn= 9780429056536}}</ref>

In Pease's view, the resultant right wing [[Populism|populist]] political movement of Angry White Males is often summarized as having experiential periods of loss both [[psychologically]] and [[sociology|sociologically]] surrounding their sense of perceived losses of the traditions of [[Man#Masculinity|men]] and their perceived "[[emasculation]]".<ref name="auto"/> Pease suggests that the [[Populism|populist]] [[Polemic|polemics]] of Angry White Males' claim to make men great again by opposing [[gender equality|equal rights]] and restoring [[Hegemonic masculinity|hegemony]] to its [[Masculism|masculinist]] right.<ref name="auto"/>

== United States ==
The term commonly refers to a political voting bloc that emerged in the early 1990s as a reaction to perceived injustices faced by white men in the face of [[affirmative action]] quotas in the workplace, much like how the [[Reagan Democrat]] bloc emerged a decade earlier.<ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.salon.com/2016/03/28/the_truth_about_donald_trumps_angry_white_men_inside_the_media_narrative_that_the_media_doesnt_understand/ |title=The truth about Donald Trump's angry white men: Inside the media narrative that the media doesn't understand |author=Heather Digby Parton |date=2016-03-28 |work=Salon }}</ref> Angry white men are characterized as having animosity toward young people, people of color, women or other minorities, and liberalism in general.<ref>{{cite book|title=[[Angry White Men|Angry White Men: American Masculinity and the End of an Era]]|first=Michael S.|last=Kimmel|date=November 5, 2013|publisher=PublicAffairs |isbn=978-1-568-58696-0}}</ref> [[Donald Trump]]'s male supporters have been described by some political commentators as angry white men.<ref>{{Cite news|first=Francis|last=Wilkinson|url=http://www.chicagotribune.com/news/opinion/commentary/ct-donald-trump-angry-white-males-20160823-story.html|title=The beginning of the end of angry white males|newspaper=[[Chicago Tribune]]|publisher=[[Tribune Publishing]]|location=Chicago, Illinois|date=August 23, 2016|access-date=October 23, 2016}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news|first=Chidanand|last=Rajghatta|url=http://economictimes.indiatimes.com/news/international/world-news/donald-trumps-vote-bank-angry-white-males-with-no-college-degrees/articleshow/53428529.cms|title=Donald Trump's vote bank: Angry white males with no college degrees|newspaper=[[The Economic Times]]|publisher=[[The Times Group]]|location=Mumbai, India|date=July 28, 2016|access-date=October 23, 2016}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|first=Kyle|last=Mantyla|url=http://www.rightwingwatch.org/post/how-angry-white-male-wayne-allyn-root-knows-that-trump-has-deep-support-among-black-voters/|title=How 'Angry White Male' Wayne Allyn Root Knows That Trump Has Deep Support Among Black Voters |website=[[Right Wing Watch]]|date=August 26, 2016|access-date=October 23, 2016}}</ref><ref>{{Cite magazine|url=https://www.gq.com/story/why-angry-white-men-love-calling-people-cucks|title=Why Angry White Men Love Calling People 'Cucks'|last=Schwartz|first=Dana|date=August 1, 2016|magazine=[[GQ]]|publisher=[[Advance Publications]]|location=New York City|access-date=October 23, 2016}}</ref>

Speaking in 2008, then-senator and future [[president-elect]] [[Barack Obama]] spoke of the small town residents left behind by successive administrations, saying that he felt it was "not surprising when they get bitter, they cling to guns or religion or antipathy toward people who aren't like them or anti-immigrant or anti-trade sentiment as a way to explain their frustrations".<ref name="wp">{{cite news |last1=Ross |first1=Janell |title=Obama revives his 'cling to guns or religion' analysis — for Donald Trump supporters |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/news/the-fix/wp/2015/12/21/obama-dusts-off-his-cling-to-guns-or-religion-idea-for-donald-trump/ |access-date=14 October 2024 |newspaper=Washington Post |date=25 November 2021}}</ref> In 2015, he referenced male [[blue-collar worker]]s having what he saw as a "justified, but just misdirected" sense of fear, frustration and anger, and believed that [[Donald Trump]]'s [[Donald Trump 2016 presidential campaign|2016 candidacy for presidency]] was taking advantage of that sentiment.<ref name="wp"/> In the [[2012 RNC]], [[South Carolina]] senator [[Lindsey Graham]] said, "The demographics race we’re losing badly. We’re not generating enough angry white guys to stay in business for the long term."<ref>{{Cite web |last=LeTourneau |first=Nancy |date=2016-03-04 |title="We're Not Generating Enough Angry White Guys" |url=https://washingtonmonthly.com/2016/03/04/were-not-generating-enough-angry-white-guys/ |access-date=2025-10-21 |website=Washington Monthly |language=en-US}}</ref>

==Australia ==
The concept also appeared during Australia's [[1998 Australian federal election|1998 federal elections]].<ref name=Sawer1999>{{Cite journal|last=Sawer|first=Marian|date=1999|title=EMILY'S LIST and angry white men: Gender wars in the nineties|journal=Journal of Australian Studies|publisher=Australia Research Institute, Curtin University of Technology|location=Perth, Australia|volume=23|issue=62|pages=1–9|doi=10.1080/14443059909387494}}</ref> New political parties appeared in that election due to the preexisting [[fathers' rights movement in Australia]]. These included the Abolish Family Support/Family Court Party and the [[Family Law Reform Party]].<ref name=Sawer1999/> Similar to the usage of the term in the United States, the Australian men categorized as angry white men opposed what they perceived as the [[Feminism|feminist]] agenda. These political parties were created as a reaction to the historic number of women elected to the House of Representatives.<ref name=Sawer1999/> Members of these groups claimed that "feminists have entrenched themselves in positions of power and influence in government and are using their power to victimise men".<ref name=Sawer1999/>

Senator [[Eric Abetz]] from the centre-right [[Liberal Party of Australia|Liberal Party]], arguing against [[Section 18C of the Racial Discrimination Act 1975]], said in 2016 that it was "passing strange" that the [[Australian Human Rights Commission]] does not seem to care about what he perceives as "racist terminology" such as angry white man, but does care if another color is used to describe someone. "One cannot help but think that the term 'white' can only refer to skin colour and therefore [you] are making reference to a skin colour [and] one assumes it must have been on the basis of race that the comment was made", he commented.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.theguardian.com/australia-news/2016/aug/15/eric-abetz-says-the-phrase-angry-white-man-is-racial-vilification|title=Eric Abetz says the phrase 'angry white man' is racial vilification|first1=Gareth|last1=Hutchens|first2=Paul|last2=Karp|date=15 August 2016|access-date=9 October 2017|newspaper=[[The Guardian]]|location=London, England}}</ref>

== In popular culture ==
[[File:Carroll O'Connor Jean Stapleton Archie and Edith Bunker 1974.JPG|thumb|Carroll O'Connor as [[Archie Bunker]] in the 1970s American television sitcom ''[[All in the Family]]'', with Jean Stapleton as his wife Edith]]
The term is applied to those believed to be opposed to the [[civil rights movement]] and [[second-wave feminism]].<ref>{{cite news|first=Hanna|last=Rosin|date=November 24, 2013|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2013/11/24/books/review/angry-white-men-by-michael-kimmel.html|title=Even Madder Men: 'Angry White Men,' by Michael Kimmel" (review)|newspaper=[[The New York Times]]|location=New York City}}</ref>

The films ''[[Joe (1970 film)|Joe]]'',<ref>{{cite magazine|first=George|last=Packer|author-link=George Packer|url=http://www.newyorker.com/online/blogs/comment/2012/02/poor-white-and-republican.html|title=Poor, White, and Republican|magazine=[[The New Yorker]]|publisher=[[Condé Nast]]|date=February 14, 2012}}</ref> ''[[Raging Bull]]'',<ref name=sun /> ''[[Falling Down]]'', ''[[Cobb (film)|Cobb]]'',<ref name=sun /> ''[[God Bless America (film)|God Bless America]]'', ''[[Taxi Driver (film)|Taxi Driver]]'', ''[[Joker (2019 film)|Joker]]'', and [[Clint Eastwood]]'s performances in ''[[Dirty Harry]]''<ref name=sun>{{cite news|first=Stephen|last=Hunter|date=February 19, 1995|url=https://www.baltimoresun.com/1995/02/19/cobb-is-latest-foray-by-hollywood-into-soul-of-a-bitter-white-male-major-league-anger/|title='Cobb' is latest foray by Hollywood into soul of a bitter white male Major-League Anger|newspaper=[[The Baltimore Sun]]|publisher=[[Tribune Publishing]]|location=Baltimore, Maryland}}</ref> and ''[[Gran Torino (film)|Gran Torino]]'' have been described as an exploration of the angry white man.<ref>{{cite news|first=Jonathan|last=Romney|url=https://www.independent.co.uk/arts-entertainment/films/reviews/gran-torino-clint-eastwood-117-mins-15-1628608.html |archive-url=https://ghostarchive.org/archive/20220507/https://www.independent.co.uk/arts-entertainment/films/reviews/gran-torino-clint-eastwood-117-mins-15-1628608.html |archive-date=May 7, 2022 |url-access=subscription |url-status=live|title=Gran Torino, Clint Eastwood: The screen legend plays an angry old man at war with the city of Detroit|newspaper=[[The Independent on Sunday]]|publisher=Independent Print, Ltd.|location=London, England|date=February 22, 2009}}{{cbignore}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|first=Ryan|last=Senaga|url=http://honoluluweekly.com/film/current-film/2009/01/angry-white-man/|title=Angry white man: Clint Eastwood channels ghosts from past films in Gran Torino|newspaper=[[Honolulu Weekly]]|date=January 14, 2009|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140202130206/http://honoluluweekly.com/film/current-film/2009/01/angry-white-man/ |archive-date=February 2, 2014 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite magazine|url=http://www.cambridgeday.com/2016/11/18/angry-white-men-on-film-seven-times-cinema-got-to-the-trump-vote-before-us/|title=Angry white men on film: Seven times cinema got to the Trump vote before us|magazine=[[Cambridge Day]]|date=November 18, 2016|access-date=March 22, 2017}}</ref> In particular, the protagonist of ''Falling Down'' (a divorced, laid-off defense worker who descends via chance and choice into a spiral of increasing rage and violence) was widely reported upon as a representative of the stereotype.<ref>{{cite book |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=_Zc0e8caLkEC |pages=61–5 |title=Critical race narratives |first1=Carl Scott |last1=Gutiérrez-Jones |publisher=[[NYU Press]]|location=New York City|year=2001 |isbn=978-0-8147-3145-1}}</ref>

The character [[Archie Bunker]] from the TV sitcoms ''[[All in the Family]]'' and ''[[Archie Bunker's Place]]'' "turned the angry white male into a cultural icon", according to [[CBS News]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.cbsnews.com/news/farewell-archie/|title=Farewell Archie|website=[[CBS News]]|publisher=[[CBS Corporation]]|location=New York City|date=June 21, 2001}}</ref> [[Walter White (Breaking Bad)|Walter White]] in the television series ''[[Breaking Bad]]'' has also been described as an "angry white male".<ref>{{cite web|first=Emily|last=Vanderwerff|url=https://www.salon.com/2013/09/22/breaking_bads_racial_politics_walter_white_angry_white_man/|title="Breaking Bad's" racial politics: Walter White, angry white man|website=[[Salon.com]]|publisher=[[Salon Media Group]]|location=New York City|date=September 22, 2013}}</ref>
